p:NIC: Nicaragua's money is issued by the Central Bank of Nicaragua, which scores 31 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed. One case runs from 2000 to 2008 and ended in an official finding. In 2007 the country's Comptroller General, the state auditor, concluded that the bank's board sold CENI certificates, paper issued to cover the collapse of banks, for less than they were worth and then raised interest rates to the benefit of the main buyer, Bancentro; the fraud is put at 500 million dollars. The Comptroller alleged criminal involvement by six men, among them former finance minister Eduardo Montealegre, who denied wrongdoing and called it a political witch hunt, and in July 2008 a special prosecutor filed charges against 39 people including him. No central bank officials are named among the accused and no court ruling is given, though former bank president Francisco Mayorga had already been found guilty in the banking scandal. The man who now runs the bank came to it from the government: Ovidio Reyes was Chief Economist at the Ministry of Finance from 2004 to 2012, became the bank's General Manager in 2012-13 and its President in January 2014, a move between two public bodies, with no private employer named. At the end of 2024 the statute governing the bank was rewritten in a week. The presidency sent the National Assembly the Ley de Administracion del Sistema Monetario y Financiero on 19 December 2024; it went to committee on 23 December during the legislative recess, was approved on 26 December and published in La Gaceta on 30 December. It repealed the bank's own organic law and the law governing the Superintendency of Banks and Other Financial Institutions, and put the two institutions, until then independent of each other, under one statute and one common board chaired by Reyes, abolishing the Superintendency's own board; Reyes was also given coordination of the Financial Analysis Unit and the deposit fund. The law's own text says the institutions keep organic, functional, administrative, financial and budgetary autonomy and their institutional specialisation. Divergentes read it the other way, writing that the law eliminates the autonomy of the monetary and financial institutions and gives plenipotentiary powers to Reyes and to the Executive, and that removing the cross-checks between supervisor and central bank removes a safeguard against political and economic bias. Article 24 obliges every person resident or domiciled in Nicaragua, national or foreign, to give the bank and the Superintendency whatever economic, financial, statistical and regulatory information they ask for. The bank did not object publicly and its president gained authority rather than losing it; what changed was that the law governing the bank was rewritten by the Executive, without consultation. Baker Tilly Nicaragua, S.A. audited the accounts for 2024, and on 27 March 2024 the printer Orell Fussli was reported to have been partly awarded a tender to print and supply the bank's banknotes, with no value or quantity given.
p:ABW: The Central Bank of Aruba, created in 1986, issues the Aruban florin and holds it at a peg to the US dollar as of December 2025. Its Central Bank Ordinance of 1991, amended through 2014, keeps the bank under the Governor of Aruba and the Minister of Finance. Section 18 has the Governor appoint the president and executive directors from a shortlist of three put up by the Supervisory Board, and suspend or dismiss them by state decree; section 19(3) allows general guidelines for their duties to be set by decree; section 23 gives him the appointment and dismissal of the supervisory directors; and section 27(1) has the Government Commissioner supervise the bank under the Minister's instructions. One case is recorded: the General Audit Chamber, reviewing the country's 2001-2004 accounts, found contributions paid into an earmarked account at the bank for the Fondo Desaroyo Aruba foundation were not accounted for completely, correctly and on time, with 16,898,503 florins paid in by the Netherlands left off the balance sheet out of a 19.3 million florin balance at the end of 2000. The president who held the post until the end of 2025 spent her working life in public bodies: Jeanette R. (Jane) Semeleer began as a management adviser at Aruba's Department of Economic Affairs, later worked at the Department of External Relations, joined the bank in 1990, was appointed Executive Director in 2000 and President in 2008, and retired on 1 December 2025; no private employer is named. Crane Currency is listed as having supplied new banknotes in 2019, on a client list in another organisation's announcement rather than a contract notice, so that is reported rather than confirmed by the bank. BNP Paribas Asset Management runs a fixed income mandate in US dollars and gives advice, and Ernst & Young audits the accounts. Aruba scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MDG: The Central Bank of Madagascar issues the country's money. Madagascar scores 32 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 0 means shielded and 100 fully exposed, which is less exposed than half of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, at 71, driven by corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks, scored 6.77 of 10 with 1 the riskiest; the Corruption Perceptions Index puts the country at 25 of 100. Written independence from government scores 0.607 of 1; the bank was set up in 1973, and of four reforms since 1970, three raised independence and one lowered it. In February 2012 the transitional government dismissed governor Frederic Rasamoely. Bank employees staged a sit-in, saying the removal went against the bank's independence, and said their strike would continue while they challenged the new governor's appointment. The present governor, Aivo Handriatiana Andrianarivelo, was appointed by the Council of Ministers on 4 January 2023, coming from the International Monetary Fund, where he had been an Executive Director and board member representing 23 African countries; he had earlier been finance director at Catholic Relief Services, managing director of the state share-management body Fonds de Portage et de Privatisation and a technical adviser in the economy and finance ministry. His profile says only that he gained earlier experience at bank level, without naming the bank or giving dates, so no private financial employer is established. One case is on record, from 2026, and it is an allegation that remains unproven. During a period of popular demonstrations it was alleged that an unnamed senior official had pressured the bank to release funds. On 21 January 2026, at Antaninarenina, Andrianarivelo denied the allegation outright, saying the bank's only clients are the commercial banks, the public Treasury and international partner organisations working on major projects, that no individual can hold an account at the bank, himself included, and that requests for disbursement from the president, prime minister or ministers are not acted on because only the public Treasury can authorise a disbursement. No amount, no date for the alleged movement of funds and no name were given. He made the remarks while signing two agreements with the security forces on guarding bank sites and escorting cash between Toamasina, Antananarivo and the bank's eleven branches. The 20,000-ariary note is produced on Giesecke+Devrient's Louisenthal Hybrid substrate from Papierfabrik Louisenthal, which makes the material rather than printing the note; the printer is not named.
p:CPV: The Bank of Cape Verde issues the escudo, and the government of Portugal guarantees it under a currency cooperation agreement signed on 13 March 1998. The rate is fixed at 110.265 Cape Verdean escudos to the euro, having started at 0.55 escudos to the Portuguese escudo. The Portuguese Treasury provides a short-term credit line of 27.5 million euros, which can rise to 45 million, with drawings capped at 5 million, and Cabo Verde must transfer reserves equal to 35 per cent of what it asks for; Banco de Portugal states the facility obliges neither it nor any euro-area institution to step in. The bank has also signed a technical assistance agreement with the World Bank Treasury's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership, becoming its 75th member, which is advisory work rather than management of its assets, and De La Rue printed the 1,000 and 2,000 escudo notes released on 15 April 2025. Its books are checked from outside by EY's Cape Verde member firm, which signed the auditor's report on the 2024 accounts and gave an opinion without qualifications on a balance sheet total of 99,898,332 thousand escudos and negative equity of 622,855 thousand escudos. The governor since 4 January 2021, Oscar Humberto Evora Santos, has moved back and forth between the bank and other public work: he joined the bank in 1991 in its studies and statistics department, worked from 1994 to 2000 on a World Bank vocational training project and then as coordinator of a UN-funded employment promotion project, returned to the bank from 2002 to 2013 as adviser and coordinator of the economic studies division, was Councillor for Finance and Business at the Municipality of Praia from 2008 to 2016 and Mayor of Praia from 2016 to 2020. No private employer is named. Who decides policy is written into its founding law, and that law was replaced in 2026: Lei n.º 70/X/2026 of 26 January 2026 revokes the 2002 Organic Law and states that the Government defines monetary and exchange rate policy with the bank collaborating, while the bank executes that policy on its own authority. The Council of Ministers appoints the Governor and Vice-Governor on the finance minister's proposal, and under article 51 they cannot be moved and may be dismissed only for ceasing to meet the requirements of office or for serious misconduct, with a right of appeal. Its law scores 0.518 of 1 for independence on a measure taken before that change, where 1 means the bank rather than the government holds the power. No case at the bank is documented, which is not proof none happened. It scores 51 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, more exposed than 96 per cent of the 194 places with a figure, with money issued, backed or fixed from abroad the main reason.
p:MRT: The Central Bank of Mauritania issues Mauritania's money, the ouguiya, and scores 30 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed; its weakest side is corruption in the country and money-laundering risk in its banks. Central Banking reported on 30 July 2004 that President Maaouiya Ould Taya had sacked the chairman of the bank, the day after sacking his whole economic team, and that Zeine Ould Zeidane, formerly an adviser to the president, was installed in his place. The report names neither the sacked chairman nor any reason and gives no calendar date, saying only that it happened on the Monday. It rests on a single account relayed from IRIN, so it is reported rather than confirmed. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank; early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. By March 2021 seven people were in pretrial detention, presumed to have taken about 1 million dollars, and supporters held a sit-in demanding a quick trial. No trial or verdict is reported. The governor since 21 January 2020, Mohamed El Cheikh El Kebir Moulaye, came to the post from ministerial office: he had held bank posts in studies, balance of payments and liquidity management, was deputy governor from 2014 to 2019, served as Minister of Employment and Vocational Training in 2007-2008 and was Minister of Economy and Industry from August 2019 until the appointment, a move between public bodies. He was also director general of PROCAPEC, the popular savings and credit funds, whose ownership the report does not state. The bank also signed an agreement with the World Bank treasury on foreign exchange reserve management, under which the treasury department provides technical assistance covering training of reserve staff, organisation of the relevant structures and the eventual setting up of a trading room; that is advice and training, not management of the money. Who prints the money is reported rather than confirmed by the bank: an industry body's profile says the 20-ouguiya polymer note launched on 28 November 2021 was made by the Canadian Bank Note Company, Limited, which is a third-party announcement rather than anything confirmed on the bank's own site. The 50-ouguiya note marking fifty years of the currency, introduced on 18 June 2023, came on three substrates, Durasafe composite by Landqart, paper with sisal by Oberthur and Hybrid by Louisenthal, while its printer is recorded as unknown.
p:OMN: The Central Bank of Oman, created in 1974, issues the Omani rial and holds it at a fixed rate, a peg, to the US dollar as of December 2025. No documented case at the bank was found, and no government pressure was reported in the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around it, with financial secrecy at 72.4 of 100. Independence written into its law scores 0.618 of 1 on one index and 0.46 on another, both measured on the law as it stood before 2025. That law has since been replaced. From 1 January 2025 Royal Decree 2/2025 issued a new Banking Law repealing the one of 2000, and Royal Decree 3/2025 issued the System of the Central Bank of Oman, a twenty-one article statute that serves as the bank's own governing act and is described as giving it legal, financial and administrative independence. The board is nonetheless made by decree: Royal Decree 4/2025 appointed a member of the ruling family as Chairman and made the Minister of Economy Deputy Chairman, with the Governor, the Undersecretary of the Ministry of Finance and the chairman of the Financial Services Authority among the members, and Royal Decree 5/2025 appointed the Governor with the rank of Minister. That Governor, Ahmed Al Musalmi, came to the bank in January 2025 from commercial banking: he had been chief executive of Sohar International Bank since 2018, and he replaced Tahir Al Amri. The appointment page does not state who owns Sohar International Bank; a separate shareholding breakdown for Sohar International Bank SAOG lists mixed ownership, with the state or government holding 11.6 per cent (Royal Court Affairs 11.6 per cent and Oman Investment Authority 4.53 per cent), private companies 17.3 per cent, public companies 11 per cent, institutions 15.6 per cent and the general public 44.5 per cent. It holds 6.7 tonnes of gold, 3.6 per cent of reserves. Oman's first polymer note, a 1-rial commemorative reported for introduction on 11 January 2026, was printed by Giesecke+Devrient; that is a commemorative, not the circulating series. Oman scores 29 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence. The Independent Auditor's Report in the bank's Annual Report 2023 is signed by KPMG at Muscat on 7 May 2024.
p:KGZ: The National Bank of the Kyrgyz Republic issues the som and holds it within 2 per cent of the US dollar. One case is recorded. In September 2005 prosecutors placed the governor, Ulan Sarbanov, under house arrest, accusing him of abuse of power for handing more than 400,000 US dollars to the deposed president Askar Akayev in 1999. Sarbanov denied wrongdoing, and Euromoney reported that his position had been insecure since Akayev was ousted in March 2005 and that politicians close to the new leader, Kurmanbek Bakiyev, had pressed for his dismissal. On 26 April 2006 Judge Esenjan Abylkasymov acquitted him and four other former finance officials, ruling that there was no crime because they had acted in the interests of the state; the prosecutor's office said it would appeal, and no appeal outcome was found. Two heads have left since: parliament approved the early resignation of Kubanychbek Bokontaev on 26 June 2024, and Melis Turgunbaev, chairman from that same day, resigned on 18 March 2026, which the report calls voluntary. Neither article gives a reason. One career move runs the other way, out of the bank and into commercial banking: Maksat Ishenbaev, a deputy chairman of the bank's board until 2007, took office on 15 January 2025 as chairman of the board of MBANK, the commercial bank OJSC Commercial Bank Kyrgyzstan, whose audited accounts filed with the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange state that a private individual, O. T. Babanov, held 97.97 per cent at 31 December 2024, with A. T. Babanova holding the same stake a year earlier, 2.03 per cent held by other physical and legal persons and no state body listed. His earlier posts include Energo Bank from 2000 to 2004, the representative office of OJSC Bank CenterCredit from 2007 to 2010, Zalkar Bank from 2010 to 2012, a leasing company and an insurance company, Bai-Tushum bank from December 2017 and the supervisory board of the Kyrgyz Stock Exchange from May 2018; the ownership of those earlier employers is not stated. Crane Currency printed the 5,000-som note introduced on 10 May 2024; Central Asian Secure Printing Typography began printing at home in September 2026, with 20- and 50-som notes entering circulation on 27 October, while an earlier attempt by Uchkun in March 2025 produced 10-som notes that never circulated. Baker Tilly Bishkek LLC audits the accounts for 2025. Kyrgyzstan scores 31 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:SYR: The Central Bank of Syria issues the Syrian pound, which moves within a band of about 5 percent against the US dollar. Basic Monetary Law No. 23 of 2002, issued in Damascus on 17 March 2002 by President Bashar al-Assad, places the bank and its policy-making council under the government. Article 1 has the Monetary and Credit Council work within the general economic directions of the state approved by the Council of Ministers. Article 8(3) has its decisions passed to the Minister of Economy and Foreign Trade, who may suspend for up to seven days any decision he considers contrary to the interest of the state and must refer a continuing disagreement to the Council of Ministers. Article 69 has the Governor appointed, and his service ended, by decree; article 2 puts the Council's non-bank seats, among them assistant ministers and the head of the State Planning Authority, in the gift of a decree; and article 71 has the Minister name the four supervising directors who sit with the Governor on the management committee. Government pressure was reported in 11 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time pressing the bank to ease and demanding that it print money. One case runs from 2005 to 2011: a Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 14 percent on banknote contracts and that the kickback returned to local decision makers. Prosecutors had told the court that former OeBS employees paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks in exchange for contracts to print money, an allegation as reported. OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Syrian official was named or tried. The governor appointed in May 2026, Safwat Raslan, came to the bank after a career largely in commercial banking abroad: he was a credit business manager at Deutsche Apotheker und Aerztebank in Germany, a consultant at EY and Capco, a banking expert at TARGOBANK and Deutsche Bank and a branch manager at Byblos Bank Syria, and his most recent post was director general of the Syrian Development Fund. No dates are given, and the ownership of those employers is not stated. Syria appoints no private audit firm: article 68(3) of the same law gives the auditing of the bank's records and accounts to the Central Organization for Financial Control, the state's own supreme audit institution. A circulating 500-pound note is printed by Goznak, the Russian state currency works. Syria scores 40 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:QAT: The Qatar Central Bank issues the riyal, held at a fixed rate to the US dollar (a peg). Its law scores 0.607 of 1 on one independence index and 0.586 on another, where 1 means the bank holds the power. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters in 2010-2018, and no documented case at the bank was found. Where the bank sits is set out in its own law and has no end date. Under Law No. 13 of 2012, issued by the Emir, the bank is a corporate body with its own capital and budget and is under the direct control of the Emir; the Governor is appointed by Emiri decision for a renewable five-year term with the rank of a minister, and the board seats representatives of the ministries responsible for finance and for trade. The Governor, Sheikh Bandar bin Mohammed bin Saoud Al-Thani, has worked only in public bodies: an early career at the bank in the Credit and Banking Supervision Section and then the Investment Department as head of trading and managing the foreign exchange reserves, establishing and then leading the Qatar Credit Bureau as its chief executive, with the Banking Risk Department added in 2014, Head of the State Audit Bureau from 2015 to 2021, and then Governor. No bank, asset manager or other private financial firm is named. It has 4 swap lines, which are agreements to borrow another central bank's currency. They include 35 billion Chinese yuan with China, with a renewal agreement dated 14 October 2026, and 15 billion US dollars' worth of lira and riyal with Turkiye, amended in 2020, whose current status is not confirmed. It holds 116.2 tonnes of gold, 26.8 per cent of reserves. The exposure score is 29 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 fully exposed. De La Rue printed the 22-riyal commemorative note issued for the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
p:TON: The National Reserve Bank of Tonga issues the pa'anga, which follows a crawling peg or a band of 1 per cent or less against the US dollar. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga Act, Chapter 16.12 in its 2020 revised edition, sets out how the government may steer it. Section 10(1) has the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, appoint five directors and the Chairman and Deputy Chairman, and section 11(1) has the Governor appointed by Cabinet on the Minister's recommendation. Section 50(1) lets the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, issue the bank written directives, and section 50(4) requires him to put any disagreement with the Board over a policy it has determined to Cabinet, which then determines the policy the bank adopts. The Governor is protected in office: under section 11(3) he may be removed by Cabinet, on the Minister's recommendation made at the Board's request, only for permanent incapacity, serious misconduct or failure to perform his duties. The present Governor, Tatafu Moeaki, was appointed on 20 December after an open recruitment process, on the Finance Minister's recommendation in consultation with the Reserve Bank Board, and his career has been in public bodies: a director of the National Reserve Bank Board from 2013 to 2016, during which he was also the Government's chief economic adviser and chief executive of the Ministry of Finance, former chief executive of the Ministry of Trade and Economic Development, World Bank liaison, Asian Development Bank Tonga country head, Member of Parliament and Minister for Finance until 10 August 2022. No commercial bank or private financial firm is named. Two cases are documented. In 2024 and 2025 Tonga's Anti-Corruption Commissioner sued the bank and its directors, alleging that a 2024 staff payment, for example $6,600 to each of 73 staff, was an unlawful bonus linked to record profit; the board had described it as a one-off anniversary payout, and on 20 November 2025 the Court of Appeal dismissed the proceedings, finding no reasonable cause of action. Between 2017 and 2019 a Senior Exchange Control Officer forged a Government bond to support another person's New Zealand visa application and asked for $2,500 pa'anga; she pleaded guilty, her employment was terminated, and on 21 May 2019 the Supreme Court of Tonga gave her a two-year sentence, fully suspended, and ordered $800 compensation. Coopers & Lybrand audited the 1993 accounts, and De La Rue printed the 100-pa'anga note in the family introduced on 4 December 2023. Tonga scores 33 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 5.5 of 15 on what it tells the public.
p:VUT: Vanuatu's money, the vatu, is issued by the Reserve Bank of Vanuatu, created in 1980 and held within a band of 2 percent or less against the Australian dollar. The country scores 36 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank; independence written into its law scores 0.498 of 1. One case is on record. An Ombudsman report of 3 July 1996 found that governor Samson Ngwele improperly signed ten bank guarantees worth 100 million US dollars in total, without the board's approval and under pressure from Finance Minister Barak Sope, breaching the Reserve Bank Act and the Leadership Code. The guarantees went to Peter Harold Swanson for a trading programme the Ombudsman called a scam, and were still in circulation when the report was written. The report commended Ngwele's later attempts to put things right; he disagreed with its adverse comments about him. The newly appointed Governor, August Letlet, came to the bank from another public body, having been Director General of the Ministry of Finance and Economic Management; the bank's own board page gives no dates for his roles and names no commercial bank or private financial firm for him or for the other three board members, whose careers it places in government, regional organisations and donor-funded programmes. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, without a date or contract value, and the 2019 accounts were audited by KPMG, a Fiji partnership.
p:GIN: Guinea's money, the Guinean franc, is issued by the Central Bank of the Republic of Guinea. The country scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and the weakest part is corruption and secrecy around the bank. In December 2021 the country's military leader, Mamadi Doumbouya, dismissed Laounceny Kaba, who had run the bank for ten years, along with the two vice-governors, Baidy Aribot and Madjou Sow, and a younger economist, Karamo Kaba, replaced him; the report of 8 December 2021 puts the removal down to how long Kaba had held the post and to his closeness to the deposed president, Alpha Conde, and says, as a report rather than a confirmed fact, that he had tried without success to win the junta's confidence. Karamo Kaba, the bank's 16th governor, came to it from asset management: from 2003 to 2021 he was Economist Strategist and then Director of Economic Research at Ecofi Investissements, described as an asset management company and a subsidiary of the Credit Cooperatif group, and before that he was a portfolio manager and financial analyst at ACOFI Gestion and an economist at the agricultural cooperative union InVivo. On 23 June 2026 the appeals chamber of Guinea's CRIEF court convicted a former governor, Bah, in his absence of embezzlement of public funds and related offences, sentencing him to five years, ordering him to repay 10.5 million US dollars taken from the bank's coffers without trace, imposing a fine of 5 billion Guinean francs and confiscating assets; his defence said the money was released on the instruction of the highest state authorities for an international humanitarian organisation. Government pressure was reported in 4 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, each time to loosen policy and to print money. KPMG S.A. audits the accounts for 2023.
p:CUW: The Central Bank of Curacao and Sint Maarten issues the Caribbean guilder, pegged to the US dollar. It scores 50 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 95% of the 194 places scored. Neither independence index codes it. Crane Currency, headquartered in Massachusetts with plants in Malta and Sweden and a supplier to more than 50 central banks, was contracted to print the new banknotes, with the Royal Canadian Mint making the coins. One case is recorded. In July 2024 a court found former president Tromp and former deputy director Laurents guilty of document forgery over a backdated 2009 loan agreement under which over $400,000 went to Tromp's pension account. It acquitted them of official bribery and money laundering, including over a $1.5 million 2015 payment from the Venezuelan company Enpiso. One career move is documented: Bob Traa became president with effect from 13 June 2019, after working for the International Monetary Fund for over 34 years, and no private employer is named. That was a temporary appointment by the Supervisory Board, pending official appointment by Curacao and Sint Maarten.
p:STP: The Central Bank of Sao Tome and Principe issues the dobra, which is pegged to the euro. One episode is recorded. In June 2006 the cabinet dismissed the governor, Maria do Carmo Silveira, a former prime minister, together with her team, saying it had found irregularities in the construction of the new central bank building, a project valued at 8 million US dollars. No detail of those irregularities and no investigation finding was given, so the claim is unproven, and the report does not mention corruption or fraud. In early December 2022 the Council of Ministers replaced governor Americo Soares de Barros with Americo d'Oliveira dos Ramos, who had been Minister of Finance in Patrice Trovoada's government between 2014 and 2018, a move from one public post to another; no private employer is named. A commemorative 50-dobra note marking 50 years of independence, introduced on 26 August 2026, was produced by Royal Joh. Enschede in the Netherlands, as the bank's own launch communication states; that is the commemorative note, not the circulating series. The country has had two systemic banking crises since 1970, and it scores 28 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, with its weak point the corruption and secrecy around it, chiefly money-laundering risk in its banks.
p:SLV: El Salvador's central bank is the Central Reserve Bank of El Salvador, and the currency is listed as both the colon and the US dollar. The IMF's 2023 classification puts the country among places with no separate legal tender of their own, using the US dollar as their anchor; legal changes made private acceptance of Bitcoin voluntary and tax payments payable only in US dollars, listed as steps taken before an IMF loan approved on 26 February 2025. One episode with parliament is recorded. In September 2020 Nicolas Martinez, president of the bank, answered a summons from a Legislative Assembly commission investigating the debt the government had taken on during the COVID-19 pandemic and how it was used, and resigned the day after appearing; no reason for the resignation is given. Deputies asked whether the release of banks' liquidity reserve was designed so banks could buy Treasury paper, and he answered that it was an autonomous decision of the banks. One career move is recorded, and it stays within the public sector: Carlos Paredes came to the presidency of the bank from the Autonomous Port Executive Commission, the National Centre for Agricultural and Forestry Technology, the National Council for Science and Technology and the Ministry of Economy. No case at the bank is documented, which does not prove none happened; Reporters Without Borders rates the situation for journalists here as very serious in its 2026 index, so the court reports a case would be found in may not exist or may not be publishable. Written independence from government scores 0.789 of 1, and no government pressure was reported in any of the 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. On its reserves, the bank's own document on international reserves management says it joined the World Bank's Reserve Advisory and Management Partnership in 2010, which it describes as advice on reserve management rather than managing a portfolio, and it names no external portfolio manager or custodian, referring only generally to external investment portfolio managers. The Corte de Cuentas de la Republica audits the accounts under a law still in force. El Salvador scores 39 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence.
p:MDA: The National Bank of Moldova issues the leu, which is held within 2 percent of the euro. Its law scores 0.861 of 1 for independence, where 1 means the bank holds the power, and it scores 30 of 100 for exposure to outside influence. Dorin Dragutanu resigned as governor on 21 September 2015 after criticism for failing to prevent about 1 billion dollars disappearing from three Moldovan banks; he blamed pressure from politicians and denied responsibility, and President Nicolae Timofti and Prime Minister Valeriu Strelet had both said he should go. The Associated Press reported the same resignation after weeks of street protests over 1.5 billion dollars that disappeared from three banks before a parliamentary election the previous November, with protesters camping in a Chisinau square since 6 September; Dragutanu accused politicians of interfering in the bank's internal affairs. On 5 March 2020 prosecutors searched the bank's headquarters and detained deputy governor Cincilei, former deputy governor Tabirta and a division head on suspicion of fraud and money laundering tied to that theft, which surfaced in 2014 and 2015 after the bank made a 13 billion leu emergency loan later turned into public debt; they also moved to arrest Dragutanu. None of it is proven. On the evening of 21 December parliament dismissed governor Octavian Armasu by 81 votes, citing insufficient and defective work on the fraud case. Armasu had come to the bank from the government: he became Governor on 30 November 2018, appointed for a seven-year term, having served before that as Moldova's Minister of Finance. A second career runs in from the auditors rather than from a bank. The bank's own biography of Constantin Schendra, appointed Deputy Governor by a parliamentary decision of 4 November 2021, records more than eight years in international audit companies: senior auditor at Ernst & Young Moldova from 2010 to 2015 and at Ernst & Young Cyprus from 2013 to 2014, then executive director at Baker Tilly Moldova from 2015 to 2018, before joining the bank as director of banking supervision in 2018. Those are private firms in professional services rather than banks or insurers. On its reserves, the bank's own page on external technical cooperation says the World Bank assists it through the Reserve Advisory and Management Program, described as technical assistance to improve management of the state's foreign exchange reserves and knowledge sharing among member states; the arrangement is advice and training rather than the management of a portfolio. KPMG Moldova SRL checks the bank's accounts from outside, for 2024 and 2023.
p:CUB: The Central Bank of Cuba issues the Cuban peso. Its exposure score is 35 of 100, where 0 means shielded from outside influence and 100 means fully exposed; that is more exposed than 66% of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around it scores 57, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 40 of 100. Written independence from government is low: 0.354 of 1 on one index (rank 153 of 155) and 0.262 on another (rank 180 of 191). On public transparency it scores 1.5 of 15 (rank 109 of 112). Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018, but the arrangement that matters here is in the law. Decree-Law 361 of 2018, issued by the Council of State and published in the Gaceta Oficial on 12 October 2018 in place of Decree-Law 172 of 1997, requires the bank to design monetary policy in step with the government's fiscal and macroeconomic aims, under an annual policy agreement signed by ministers. It has no end date. Its notes are printed by Goznak: the 200-peso note dated 2024 and the 50-peso note dated 2025 are recorded as carrying that printer, identified from the notes themselves rather than announced by the bank, so it is reported rather than confirmed. One case is documented, and it is still under investigation: in late September 2026 an investigation in Santiago de Cuba concerned workers at two state banks, Banco Popular de Ahorro and BANDEC, both supervised by the Banco Central de Cuba, with reports saying the workers handed out cash in exchange for electronic transfers, charging commissions of between 30 and 50 per cent, acting together with self-employed people. Cash, banknote counting machines, magnetic cards and documents were reported seized, and no amounts, names or number of detainees were made public. The central bank's Minister-President, Juana Lilia Delgado Portal, issued an official note rejecting the conduct, ordering that any complaint be investigated without delay, and calling for administrative, labour and criminal responsibility to be established, internal controls strengthened and whistleblowers protected. No charges or outcomes had been announced.
p:AZE: The Central Bank of the Republic of Azerbaijan issues the manat, held at a de facto fixed rate against the US dollar. It scores 31 of 100 for exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, with corruption and secrecy around it at 62. On 12 April 2022 parliament approved President Ilham Aliyev's proposal to replace governor Elman Rustamov, in post since 1995, with Taleh Kazimov, head of Pasha Bank; Rustamov became adviser to the prime minister, and no official reason and no statement from him were reported. One career move is documented, and it is Kazimov's: at the private PASHA Bank, set up in 2007, he rose from risk manager to chief executive officer and then chairman, with no years given for those posts, and he then became governor of the central bank on the parliamentary vote reported on 18 April 2022. Two cases are documented. A Vienna court found that the Austrian banknote printer OeBS had overcharged the bank by 20 per cent on banknote contracts and that the kickback went back to local decision makers; OeBS managers were convicted in 2014 and again on retrial in 2018, and no Azerbaijani official was named or tried. Austrian prosecutors also told a court that former OeBS employees had paid bribes to officials at Syrian and Azerbaijani banks for printing contracts, which stands as a prosecution allegation. In September 2009 a Baku court sentenced six former officers of the bank to between a two-year suspended sentence and eight years for abuse of power and embezzling 1.4 million manat between 2003 and 2008. Who prints the money now is reported rather than confirmed by the bank: an industry association's per-note profile of the renewed 50-manat banknote lists G+D Currency Development GmbH, part of Giesecke+Devrient, as the printer and Papierfabrik Louisenthal GmbH as the supplier of the paper it is printed on. KPMG Audit Azerbaijan LLC audits the accounts for 2025, and the bank holds no gold.
p:HTI: The Bank of the Republic of Haiti, created in 1979, issues the gourde, held at a de facto peg to the US dollar as of December 2025; the dollar is also listed as a currency there. One case is recorded. In April 2004 justice minister Bernard Gousse barred Venel Joseph, a former governor of the bank, from leaving the country, naming him among 37 former officials to be kept available for investigations into crimes alleged against the government of ousted president Jean-Bertrand Aristide, and calling the travel ban an insurance policy. What conduct at the bank, if any, was being looked into is not reported, and no charge and no finding followed. The bank has also been called before parliament: the Senate's Economy and Finance commission summoned governor Charles Castel, with Ronald Baudin, Minister of Economy and Finance, to appear on Wednesday 1 June 2011 and answer questions about new taxes of 1.50 US dollars per money transfer and 5 cents a minute on incoming international calls. Government pressure was reported in 0 of 37 quarters from 2010 to 2018. On the printing of the money, a Haitian news outlet reports that the bank ordered a reprint of 30 million 10-gourde notes from Oberthur Fiduciaire S.A.S. for 845,000 euros; that comes from the outlet rather than from any announcement by the bank, so it is reported rather than confirmed. KPMG S.A. and the firm Merove-Pierre - Cabinet d'Experts-Comptables audit the accounts jointly, their report covering the year ended 30 September 2021. Haiti's exposure score is 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, more exposed than 72 per cent of 194 places. Corruption and secrecy around the bank scores 82, with a Corruption Perceptions Index score of 16 of 100 and money-laundering risk of 8.12 of 10, rank 2 of 177 where 1 is riskiest.
